title: Preparing for Qminers Algo Trade Arena hackathon

messages.content:
i will be participating in this hackathon

https://arena.qminers.com/

plus some new email info:

```
Hi!

You're among the 200+ participants joining the first-ever Algo Trade Arena hackathon! We are happy to have you on board!

The race for the final spots was fierce, and plenty of disappointed students are on the waiting list. If you already know your plans have changed and you won't be able to attend, please let us know straight away so we can offer your spot to someone else.

The same applies if anything changes later, even in the final days before the competition.

What do you need to know now?

The schedule is ready!
Saturday
08:00–09:00 team arrival / registration
09:00–09:30 opening ceremony
09:30–10:30 workshop

12:00–13:00 lunch break

We need to confirm your student status. If you haven't already done so, please send us your university email address or another proof that you're currently a student. You have until October 15th. If we do not receive your university email or other verification by then, your whole team will be disqualified.
All participants must be aged 18 or over. If we've asked you to confirm your age (for example, because you're part of a secondary school team) and you haven't done so yet, please do. The deadline is the same: October 15th.
A reminder: the competition is strictly in person. There will be no way to participate off-site. Participants may leave for a while to rest or sleep, but at least one member of each team must always be on-site. Plan your time accordingly.
Need some changes to your team? At this point, the only change we can accept is swapping one team member for another (under same conditions). Adding new members is no longer possible, and removing a member is only possible after consulting us first. If you need to make any change, just reply to this email and we'll sort it out together.
Food and drinks
Coffee, tea and water will be available throughout the competition. We'll also provide lunch, dinner, midnight refreshments, and a proper breakfast and light lunch the following day. If you think you might still get hungry, bring some protein bars or other snacks to keep you going.

Sleep and getting around
We've tried our best to make it possible for you to bring sleeping bags and mats, but unfortunately the building management has strict rules about this and they will not be allowed. Prepare for hardcore mode... or book some accommodation nearby and take turns with your team members. It's up to you.

What else?
You will get one last email from us approximately one week before the event. We will clarify the details about getting there and parking, and give final instructions for the competition.

If you have any questions in the meantime, just reply to this email.

Start warming up your algorithms, and see you at the Arena!
```

how would you reccomend me to prepare for it

A month out (event is November 7) is a good amount of time to prepare. Here's what we know about the format: Qminers will simulate a realistic exchange and provide a simple API, and your task is to understand market dynamics and build a trading algorithm that earns profit. The simulated exchange mimics a limit order book, without many real-world operational complexities. There will be 4 rounds of 5 hours each, starting with a forgiving market to learn the basics, building up to a sophisticated finale. A third-party listing says it's a Python trading algorithm, which suits your background, though I'd confirm that in the final email.

**First, the admin.** Send your university email for student verification before October 15 if you haven't. Missing it disqualifies your whole team.

**Learn order book mechanics until they're second nature.** You should be comfortable with bid/ask, spread, mid price, microprice (mid weighted by size on each side), order book imbalance, price-time priority, and the difference between taking liquidity with market orders and providing it with limit orders. Also learn realized vs. unrealized PnL, inventory risk, and adverse selection: why your limit orders tend to fill just before the price moves against you. Most losing bots in these competitions fail because of that last one.

**Know the standard strategy families.** In simulated LOB competitions, the winners usually rely on a few things:
- **Market making:** quote both sides around a fair value and skew your quotes based on inventory. The Avellaneda–Stoikov paper is the classic reference.
- **Mean reversion or momentum** on the fair-value signal.
- **Arbitrage between related instruments**, if there are several products, such as a basket and its components.
- **Exploiting simulated bots.** Simulated markets are driven by bots with exploitable patterns, so a lot of edge comes from staring at the data and spotting them.

**Practice on IMC Prosperity.** It's the closest public analogue: Python bots, an order book sim, progressive rounds. Top teams have published detailed write-ups and code on GitHub for the 2023–2025 editions. Reading three or four of them is probably the highest-value prep you can do. Optiver's Ready Trader Go archives are also useful.

**Build your toolkit before the event.** This is where your backend/data experience pays off. You can't write against the real API yet, so build around a thin adapter layer you can plug into on the day:
- **State tracking:** position, open orders, fills, and PnL, reconciled against what the exchange reports.
- **Risk guardrails:** position limits, max order size, and a kill switch. In round 1, not blowing up beats being clever.
- **Logging:** record every book snapshot, trade, and your own order to disk (Parquet or SQLite).
- **Replay and backtest harness:** test strategy changes on logged data between rounds.
- **Analysis notebook:** quick plots of mid price, your fills, inventory, and PnL over time.

The 5-hour rounds with breaks in between are clearly designed so that teams who log well in round N win round N+1. Also pre-install your whole environment and don't rely on venue Wi-Fi for pip installs.

**Use the playground slot (10:30–12:00) for testing.** Confirm order types, fees, position limits, rate limits, latency, and especially the scoring metric. Is it pure PnL or risk-adjusted? That changes how aggressive you should be.

**Plan team roles and sleep.** A split that works well: one person owns infrastructure and the API connection, one does data analysis and signal research, one tunes the strategy, and everyone can step in for the others. Round 3 (01:00–06:00) will be the hardest. Decide in advance who sleeps when, since at least one person must stay on-site. Living in Prague, you might be able to rotate home if the commute works; otherwise book something near the venue.

**What to bring:** laptop and charger, an extension cord (outlets run out fast), headphones, a warm layer, snacks, and basic toiletries for the morning.

I can help you build that pre-event skeleton: a tiny local order book simulator with a few dummy bots, plus a bot framework with state tracking, logging, and a basic inventory-skewed market maker. Then you'd show up with something already tested.

messages.content: can you give me a more strucutred learning plan? maybe also with some references

Here's a four-week plan running up to November 7. It assumes a few hours per week and front-loads theory so the last two weeks are hands-on.

## Week 1 (Oct 8–14): Market microstructure foundations

**Goal:** understand exactly what happens when an order hits a limit order book.

**Topics:**
- How a limit order book works: price-time priority, partial fills, cancellations
- Spread, mid price, microprice, depth, order book imbalance
- Market vs. limit orders, and who pays the spread
- Adverse selection: why informed flow hurts market makers
- PnL accounting: realized vs. unrealized PnL, mark-to-market, inventory

**References:**
- Larry Harris, *Trading and Exchanges*: the standard plain-language intro to how markets work. Read the chapters on order types, market makers, and informed traders.
- Gould et al., "Limit Order Books" (2013, *Quantitative Finance*): a survey paper with a clean formal description of LOB mechanics.
- Bouchaud, Bonart, Donier & Gould, *Trades, Quotes and Prices* (2018): more advanced. Skim the order book and price impact chapters.

**Exercise:** write a minimal order book matching engine in Python (add, cancel, and match with price-time priority). It's a couple of hours of work and makes everything concrete. It also becomes the core of your local simulator.

## Week 2 (Oct 15–21): Strategies and signals

**Goal:** know the main strategy families and when each works.

**Topics:**
- **Market making:** quoting around fair value, spread width, inventory skew, position limits
- **Fair value estimation:** mid vs. microprice vs. EMAs, plus order flow imbalance as a short-term signal
- **Mean reversion and momentum** on that signal
- **Relative value:** pairs trading and basket-vs-components arbitrage, in case the sim has multiple instruments
- **Taking vs. making:** when to cross the spread because the edge is large enough

**References:**
- Avellaneda & Stoikov, "High-frequency trading in a limit order book" (2008): the classic market-making model. Understand the intuition behind the reservation price and inventory skew; you don't need the full stochastic control derivation.
- Guéant, Lehalle & Fernandez-Tapia, "Dealing with the inventory risk" (2013): a practical extension of Avellaneda–Stoikov with closed-form approximations.
- Stoikov, "The Micro-Price" (2018): a better fair-value estimate than the mid.
- Cont, Kukanov & Stoikov, "The Price Impact of Order Book Events" (2014): introduces order flow imbalance (OFI), one of the most robust short-term signals.
- Cartea, Jaimungal & Penalva, *Algorithmic and High-Frequency Trading*: use as a reference for market making and execution chapters, not a cover-to-cover read.

## Week 3 (Oct 22–28): Learn from IMC Prosperity and build tooling

**Goal:** see how top teams approach this exact type of competition, and build your own framework.

**Write-ups to study:**
- Research and trading algorithms for team Linear Utility, which placed second in IMC Prosperity 2 (GitHub: `ericcccsliu/imc-prosperity-2`). The README is one of the best explanations of how a strong team thinks round by round.
- Alpha Animals writeups and algorithm for IMC Prosperity 3 (9th Global, 2nd USA, Peak 2nd Global) (GitHub: `CarterT27/imc-prosperity-3`).
- jmerle's open-source Prosperity backtester and visualizer on GitHub, to see what good tooling looks like.

As you read, note how they estimated fair value, how they managed inventory, what they found by exploring the data, and where they lost money. The Prosperity 3 winner said his team came in prepared, with extensive tooling, better automation, and the lessons of two previous editions behind them. That's the lesson for a 24-hour event too.

**Build:**
- **Bot framework:** an exchange adapter interface, state tracker (positions, orders, fills, PnL), risk limits, and a kill switch
- **Logging:** every book update, trade, and your own actions, saved to Parquet or SQLite
- **Local simulator:** your Week 1 matching engine plus a few dummy bots (a noise trader, a trend follower, a simple market maker)
- **Analysis notebook:** plots of mid price, fills, inventory, and PnL over time

**Exercise:** download the Prosperity historical data from one of those repos and build a market maker that is profitable in your backtester.

## Week 4 (Oct 29–Nov 6): Dry run and team prep

**Goal:** arrive with tested code and a clear plan.

**Tasks:**
- Run a full mock round: 5 hours on your simulator, with someone changing the market's behavior halfway through without telling the others.
- Practice the between-rounds workflow: load logs, find what lost money, patch, and redeploy within an hour.
- Decide team roles (infrastructure, research, strategy) and the sleep rotation for round 3.
- Freeze your environment: pinned requirements, pre-downloaded packages, everything working offline.
- Read the final organizer email carefully (expected around Oct 31) and adapt the adapter layer to whatever API details they share.

## Optional extras if you have more time

- **Optiver's Ready Trader Go** materials on GitHub: another market-making competition with a similar structure.
- **Probability and expected value practice:** *Heard on the Street* (Crack) or *A Practical Guide to Quantitative Finance Interviews* (Zhou). This is less directly relevant to the bot, but it sharpens the quick EV reasoning you'll use when deciding whether a trade is worth it.

If you want, I can help with the Week 1 matching engine or the Week 3 framework skeleton.
